narrative:
The model estimated a 51% chance that you would be a bad credit risk, meaning it judged the likelihood of repayment problems as slightly more than half. Because that crossed the bank’s threshold, your application was denied.

The strongest reason was your checking account status: having a negative balance below 0 DM pushed the assessment toward bad credit more than any other factor. This is uncommon among approved applicants—most have no overdraft or a positive balance—so it raised concern about your available funds. The second strongest factor was your credit history: being recorded as no credits/all paid pushed the assessment toward bad credit. Only about 1% of approved applicants share this pattern, so your record appeared too thin to demonstrate reliable repayment. Working in your favor was your property status: owning real estate pushed the assessment toward good credit, but it was not enough to offset the two stronger concerns. Your requested amount and duration were below the approved applicants’ averages, which also helped, but they were less influential here.

To improve your chances, speak with the bank about what evidence would strengthen a future application. Focus on clearing the overdraft and maintaining a positive checking balance, and build a documented repayment history, such as a small loan or credit facility paid on time. Ask whether adding a guarantor or co-applicant and providing stable income documentation could support a reconsideration, and reapply once those steps are in place.
